newsitem.title: USA: General Motors increases share buyback program.
newsitem.headline: General Motors increases share buyback program.

text.p: General Motors Corp., moving to return more of its growing cash hoard to shareholders, said Monday it will buy back an additional $2.5 billion worth of its common stock over the next 12 months.

The widely anticipated action follows the completion of an initial $2.5 billion repurchase program started in January. GM said it bought back 43.7 million shares of the parent company's $1-2/3 par-value common stock in just over six months.
GM also has class H stock which is tied to its Hughes Electronics Corp. subsidiary.
But the automaker did not raise its quarterly common stock dividend, declaring an unchanged payout of 50 cents a share, payable Sept. 10 to shareholders of record on Aug. 14.
GM shares were off $1.875 at $62.625 on the New York Stock Exchange shortly after midday as investors took profits from strong gains last week of nearly $6.
"The stock's been a monster mover the past week, so its just giving a little bit back," said auto analyst Nicholas Colas of CS First Boston.
He added that the increased repurchase program was fully expected by the market, but the lack of a dividend increase may have disappointed some investors.

Despite two strikes that cost it $490 million in lost earnings, GM still ended the second quarter with $14.9 billion in cash and marketable securities, compared with $13 billion a year earlier and $14.6 billion on March 31, 1997.
"GM's cash position is strong," GM Chairman Jack Smith said in a statement. "We believe that stock repurchase programs are a great way to return excess cash directly to stockholders."

"We expect to consider additional programs in the future, within the framework of the investment requirements to maintain and grow the business, the overall business climate, and our cash position going forward," Smith added.
GM said it will make the stock repurchases over a 12-month period principally through open market transactions, and would represent about 5 percent of the parent company's common stock.

"We'll continue to review the dividend rate quarterly, keeping in mind that our priority here is to provide GM shareholders with a competitive dividend that is sustainable throughout the business cycle," Smith said.

GM had 721.4 million shares of $1-2/3 common stock at the close of the second quarter, down from 756 million shares at the end of 1996. The 4.6 percent reduction was attributed to stock repurchased since January through open market transactions.

GM and Chrysler Corp. both have active share repurchase programs among Detroit automakers. Ford Motor Co., which also has a growing cash reserve, also is widely expected by Wall Street analysts to announce a buyback program in the near future.
